y-m-16-01.title: Testing Hajun's ‘if you multiply by any number the same’
y-m-16-01.topic: Division of decimals: the quotient when both numbers are changed together
y-m-16-01.goal: Test, with examples in a table, the claim that the quotient stays the same even if the dividend and divisor are changed together, and state what doubts remain even as examples increase and the condition under which it holds (the same number that is not 0).
y-m-16-01.material:
Hajun said, “It's easier to calculate if you multiply the dividend and the divisor both by 10. 4.8 ÷ 0.6 can be changed to 48 ÷ 6, and the quotient stays the same. Not just 10, but if you just multiply by any number the same, the quotient stays the same!” Hajun made the table below. (4.8 is read ‘four point eight’ and 0.6 is read ‘zero point six.’)
Multiplied by / Dividend / Divisor / Quotient
1 / 4.8 / 0.6 / 8
10 / 48 / 6 / 8
100 / 480 / 60 / 8
5 / 24 / 3 / 8
y-m-16-01.thinking.0: Knowing that a few examples do not prove ‘all cases’
y-m-16-01.thinking.1: Fixing the condition of a claim using new information
y-m-16-01.thinking.2: Thinking of kinds of numbers that have not been tested
y-m-16-01.prereq.0: Writing numbers that are a one-decimal-place number multiplied by 10 or 100
y-m-16-01.prereq.1: The words dividend, divisor, and quotient in a division equation
y-m-16-01.s.s1.prompt: After looking at the table, how will you judge Hajun's last statement (‘if you just multiply by any number the same, the quotient stays the same’)?
y-m-16-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write side by side what kinds of numbers the multiplied numbers in the table are.
y-m-16-01.s.s1.hint.1: Choose one multiplier that is not in the table and multiply 4.8 and 0.6 by it yourself.
y-m-16-01.s.s1.o.a: The quotient was 8 all four times, so it seems right, and it seems there is no need to test more
y-m-16-01.s.s1.r.a: You settled ‘any number’ just because all four examples were right. Look at what kinds of numbers appear in the table and whether there are kinds that did not appear.
y-m-16-01.s.s1.o.b: So far it looks right, but the multipliers are only natural numbers, so I want to test other kinds of numbers too
y-m-16-01.s.s1.r.b: You looked at what kinds of numbers the multipliers in the table are and thought of the cases not tested. This is the attitude of looking for what to test before settling a judgment.
y-m-16-01.s.s1.o.c: The table has only 4.8 ÷ 0.6, so I will judge after finding out whether it works for other divisions too
y-m-16-01.s.s1.r.c: You pointed out that the table covers only one division. It would be even better to look at the kinds of multipliers too.
y-m-16-01.s.s1.o.d: Multiplying makes numbers bigger, so the quotient seems to get bigger too, and Hajun's statement seems wrong
y-m-16-01.s.s1.r.d: It is not only the dividend that got bigger; the divisor got bigger together with it. First look at how the quotient changed in the table.
y-m-16-01.s.s1.explain: The table has only the multipliers 1, 5, 10, and 100, and only one division. Even if many examples are right, there are still numbers not yet tested (numbers less than 1, 0, and so on) and other divisions. ‘It seems right’ and ‘it is always right’ are different.
y-m-16-01.s.s1.acc.0: The point that the table covers only 4.8 ÷ 0.6 is also a valid doubt. If you also look at the kinds of multipliers, what to test becomes clearer.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.prompt: New information comes out one piece at a time. Each time, choose how you will view Hajun's statement.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.hint.0: Read each piece of information and write in one line ‘which part of Hajun's statement this information bumps into.’
y-m-16-01.s.s2.hint.1: Put ‘any number’ and ‘the same’ from Hajun's statement into the new information one at a time and calculate for yourself.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.0.info: Hajun tried the multiplier 0.5 too. 4.8 × 0.5 = 2.4 and 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.3, so 2.4 ÷ 0.3 = 8. He tried 1000 too, and 4800 ÷ 600 = 8. 6 ÷ 0.4 = 15 and 60 ÷ 4 = 15 were also right.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.0.ask: How do you view Hajun's statement now?
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.0.after: Your trust grew because the right examples increased. But having many examples is different from being right in all cases, so you need to keep checking whether there is an exception.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.0.o.a: There are more reasons to trust it. Still, to say ‘all numbers,’ we need to check for exceptions further
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.0.r.a: You also thought that more examples raise your trust, but whether an exception remains has to be checked separately.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.0.o.b: It was right for many kinds of numbers, so it is now proved to be right in all cases
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.0.r.b: The kinds of numbers tested have increased, but not every number has been tested. There are still numbers not yet tested.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.0.o.c: The more examples there are, the stranger it is. It must be wrong, as I first thought
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.0.r.c: Even though all the new examples were right, you did not change your first thought. Bring the new data into your judgment.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.0.o.d: There are many examples now, so there is nothing more to look at and no need to think more
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.0.r.d: Having many right examples is different from knowing the reason. We still don't know when it fails.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.1.info: Hajun's younger sibling asked, “What if the multiplier is 0?” 4.8 × 0 = 0 and 0.6 × 0 = 0, so the expression becomes 0 ÷ 0. You cannot divide by 0.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.1.ask: How would be a good way to fix Hajun's statement?
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.1.after: When the multiplier is 0, it becomes 0 ÷ 0 and the expression does not hold. If you change the statement to ‘if you multiply by a number that is not 0,’ it also fits the examples so far.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.1.o.a: Change ‘any number’ to ‘a number that is not 0’
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.1.r.a: With the new information you found the range in which the statement is right and added a condition to the statement.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.1.o.b: 0 is too special a number, so leave it out of mind and keep Hajun's statement as it is
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.1.r.b: When the multiplier is 0 the expression cannot be formed, but the statement says ‘any number,’ so it is not right. You should state exactly the range in which the statement is right.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.1.o.c: 0 doesn't work, so say this method is a method that cannot be used
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.1.r.c: Except for 0, all the earlier examples were right. Throwing away the whole method is going too far.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.1.o.d: Add that when the multiplier is 0, the quotient becomes 0
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.1.r.d: If you multiply by 0, the divisor also becomes 0, so you cannot find a quotient. The quotient does not become 0.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.2.info: This time Hajun's younger sibling multiplied the dividend 4.8 by 100 and the divisor 0.6 by 10. It became 480 ÷ 6 = 80, so the quotient was not 8.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.2.ask: Is the word ‘the same’ in Hajun's statement really needed?
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.2.after: If the numbers multiplied onto the two numbers are different, the quotient changes (480 ÷ 6 = 80). So the statement becomes ‘if you multiply both numbers by the same number that is not 0, the quotient stays the same.’
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.2.o.a: It is needed. If the numbers multiplied onto the two numbers are different, the quotient can change
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.2.r.a: You found the reason ‘the same’ is needed from an example where the multipliers are different.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.2.o.b: It is not needed. 480 ÷ 6 = 80 must be a calculation mistake
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.2.r.b: 480 ÷ 6 is indeed 80. Before blaming a mistake, calculate it again yourself.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.2.o.c: It is not needed. If you multiply only by numbers that are not 0, the quotient is the same however you multiply
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.2.r.c: The earlier examples were cases where the same number was multiplied onto both. An example where different numbers are multiplied comes up for the first time now.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.2.o.d: It is needed. But the bigger the number multiplied onto the divisor, the bigger the quotient gets
y-m-16-01.s.s2.st.2.r.d: If you make the divisor bigger, the quotient gets smaller. Think about 4.8 ÷ 6, where only the divisor is multiplied by 10.
y-m-16-01.s.s2.reflect: How did the thought that started as ‘it seems right’ change each time it met new information? What grew as examples increased, and what was not resolved even as examples increased and could be known only with new information?
y-m-16-01.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Hajun's statement exactly. Write it with the conditions, and also write an example you checked with one division that is not 4.8 ÷ 0.6.
y-m-16-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write one sentence each on what the problem was with the second and the third pieces of information, and then put them together.
y-m-16-01.s.s3.hint.1: Choose one division that fits your corrected statement, multiply both numbers by the same number, and compare the quotients.
y-m-16-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If ..., the quotient stays the same. For example ...
y-m-16-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In my statement, are both ‘not 0’ and ‘the same for both numbers’ clear?
y-m-16-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you calculate the example you gave yourself and check that the two quotients are the same?
y-m-16-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you know and write that multiplying by different numbers can change the quotient?
y-m-16-01.s.s3.model.0: If you multiply both the dividend and the divisor by the same number that is not 0, the quotient stays the same. For example, 6 ÷ 0.4 = 15, and multiplying both by 10 gives 60 ÷ 4, which is also 15.
y-m-16-01.s.s3.model.1: As long as the multiplier is not 0, multiplying both numbers by the same number doesn't change the quotient. I checked 9 ÷ 1.5 = 6 and 90 ÷ 15 = 6.
y-m-16-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: A number other than 10 can be used in an example too (multiplying by 10 turns 1.5 into 15).

y-m-16-02.title: Checking the amount of water left after pouring into cups
y-m-16-02.topic: Division of decimals: the remainder in a division with a remainder
y-m-16-02.goal: In a decimal division where the quotient is found to the natural-number place, find the line where the size of the remainder is wrong, choose the ways to check whether the remainder is right, and make your own division problem with a remainder.
y-m-16-02.material: Doyun wants to pour 8.6 L of water into 0.4 L cups, filling each cup completely. He found the quotient only to the natural-number place and also found the remainder (the amount of water left over). Below is Doyun's solution. (Count the line numbers from 1.)
y-m-16-02.thinking.0: Finding the first wrong line in a solution
y-m-16-02.thinking.1: Comparing ways to check whether a result is right
y-m-16-02.thinking.2: Making a problem that reveals an error
y-m-16-02.prereq.0: Multiplying a one-decimal-place number by a natural number
y-m-16-02.prereq.1: Division of natural numbers with a remainder (quotient, remainder, the remainder is smaller than the divisor)
y-m-16-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Doyun's solution that is wrong.
y-m-16-02.s.s1.hint.0: Follow how each line came from the line just before it, and mark the lines where the numbers changed.
y-m-16-02.s.s1.hint.1: In line 2, both numbers were multiplied by 10. Compare whether the quotient and remainder that came after that are the same as the quotient and remainder of the original division.
y-m-16-02.s.s1.line.0: In 8.6 ÷ 0.4, find the quotient only to the natural-number place and find the remainder too.
y-m-16-02.s.s1.line.1: Multiply the dividend 8.6 and the divisor 0.4 both by 10 to change it to 86 ÷ 4.
y-m-16-02.s.s1.line.3: Therefore the quotient of 8.6 ÷ 0.4 is 21 and the remainder is 2.
y-m-16-02.s.s1.line.4: Answer: 21 cups are filled completely and 2 L of water is left over.
y-m-16-02.s.s1.explain: The first wrong place is line 4. Since both numbers were multiplied by 10 in line 2, the remainder 2 of 86 ÷ 4 is ‘10 times the original remainder.’ So the remainder of 8.6 ÷ 0.4 is 0.2. The calculation is right up to line 3, and line 5 is wrong because it follows line 4.
y-m-16-02.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the ways that can check whether Doyun's answer ‘21 cups, 2 L of water left’ is right.
y-m-16-02.s.s2.hint.0: Recall the equation used to check a division with a remainder (the equation that makes the dividend from the divisor, quotient, and remainder).
y-m-16-02.s.s2.hint.1: Try each way yourself with Doyun's numbers and check whether anything odd shows up.
y-m-16-02.s.s2.o.a: He filled 21, so compare which is bigger, 21 or 8.6
y-m-16-02.s.s2.r.a: 0.4 L is a cup smaller than 1 L, so it is not odd for the number of cups to be larger than the amount of water (the number showing L). This comparison cannot reveal the error.
y-m-16-02.s.s2.o.b: Compare whether the 2 L of leftover water is bigger than the size of one cup, 0.4 L
y-m-16-02.s.s2.r.b: This used the rule that the remainder must be smaller than the divisor. It also tells you whether you could fill more cups with the leftover water.
y-m-16-02.s.s2.o.c: Calculate 86 ÷ 4 again and check that 21 remainder 2 is right
y-m-16-02.s.s2.r.c: This repeated the same calculation. 86 ÷ 4 itself is right, so an error related to the decimal point does not show up with this method.
y-m-16-02.s.s2.o.d: Calculate 0.4 × 21 + 2 and check whether it equals 8.6
y-m-16-02.s.s2.r.d: This used the relation divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend.
y-m-16-02.s.s2.explain: The remainder must be smaller than the divisor, but 2 L is bigger than 0.4 L. Also, 0.4 × 21 + 2 = 10.4, which is different from 8.6. It should be 0.4 × 21 + 0.2 = 8.6, so the remainder is 0.2 L. Recalculating 86 ÷ 4 only repeats the same solution, so it cannot find this error.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.prompt: Make a problem that is easy to get wrong if you solve it the same way as Doyun. The dividend a and the divisor b are numbers with up to one decimal place, a must be 1 or more, and b must be greater than 0 and less than 1. When you find the quotient of a ÷ b to the natural-number place, make 3 different problems whose quotient is from 10 to 40 and whose remainder is not 0.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.hint.0: Choose b first, then change a to find cases where the quotient is from 10 to 40 and it does not divide evenly.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.hint.1: Once you choose a candidate, change it to a division of natural numbers by multiplying both numbers by 10, and check whether the remainder is 0.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.ok.c1: a is 1 or more, and a and b are numbers with up to one decimal place.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.fail.c1: a must be 1 or more, b must be a number greater than 0, and both numbers must be written with only up to one decimal place.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.fail.c2: The divisor b is not less than 1.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.ok.c3: It does not divide evenly, so there is a remainder.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.fail.c3: It divides evenly, so there is no remainder. Change it to numbers that leave a remainder.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.ok.c4: The quotient (the natural-number part) is from 10 to 40.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.fail.c4: The quotient (the natural-number part) is not from 10 to 40.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.explain: For example, 8.6 ÷ 0.4 is quotient 21 remainder 0.2, 7.3 ÷ 0.6 is quotient 12 remainder 0.1, and 9.5 ÷ 0.7 is quotient 13 remainder 0.4. If you calculate after multiplying both numbers by 10, the remainder also becomes 10 times as big, so you must bring the remainder back to its original size.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.because.prompt: Choose one of the problems you made, write its quotient and remainder, and write in one or two sentences how you checked that the remainder is right.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.because.hint.0: Choose one problem you made, write the division with both numbers multiplied by 10, and write how you will bring the remainder back to its original size.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.because.hint.1: Calculate divisor × quotient + remainder and check whether it equals the dividend.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.because.placeholder: e.g. ...÷... is quotient ... remainder .... The check is ...
y-m-16-02.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Is the remainder I wrote smaller than the divisor?
y-m-16-02.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you bring the remainder from the multiplied-by-10 calculation back to its original size?
y-m-16-02.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Did you calculate ‘divisor × quotient + remainder’ yourself?
y-m-16-02.s.s3.because.model.0: 7.3 ÷ 0.6 is quotient 12 remainder 0.1. 0.6 × 12 = 7.2, and adding 0.1 gives 7.3, and the remainder 0.1 is smaller than 0.6.
y-m-16-02.s.s3.because.model.1: 9.5 ÷ 0.7 = 13 remainder 0.4. I checked by calculating whether 0.7 × 13 + 0.4 = 9.5.

y-m-16-03.title: Collecting fractions that lie between 0.6 and 3/4
y-m-16-03.topic: Comparing the sizes of fractions and decimals: numbers between two numbers
y-m-16-03.goal: Evaluate several ways of comparing the sizes of fractions and decimals, and find, to fit the conditions, irreducible fractions that lie between two numbers.
y-m-16-03.material:
Seoyeon wants to collect fraction cards that lie between 0.6 and 3/4 (three fourths). First, three friends each said, using their own method, whether 7/12 (seven twelfths) is greater or less than 0.6.
Siu: “In 7/12 the numerator 7 is greater than the 6 in 0.6, so 7/12 is bigger.”
Hayoon: “If you divide 7 by 12 you get 0.58333…. Compared with 0.6, 7/12 is smaller.”
Dohyun: “I changed 0.6 to 3/5 and put it over a common denominator of 60 with 7/12. It's 35/60 and 36/60, so 0.6 is bigger.”
Jihu: “If you change 0.6 into twelfths, it is 7.2/12. Comparing the numerators 7 and 7.2, 7/12 is smaller.”
y-m-16-03.thinking.1: Thinking that there are many numbers between two numbers
y-m-16-03.thinking.2: Making several examples that satisfy the conditions
y-m-16-03.prereq.0: Writing fractions as decimals and decimals as fractions
y-m-16-03.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of fractions by finding a common denominator
y-m-16-03.prereq.2: Reducing to write an irreducible fraction
y-m-16-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the suitable ways to compare the sizes of 7/12 and 0.6.
y-m-16-03.s.s1.hint.0: For each of the four methods, check whether it changed the two numbers into the ‘same form.’
y-m-16-03.s.s1.hint.1: Choose one method and apply it yourself to 7/12 and 0.6, and compare whether it matches the results of the other methods.
y-m-16-03.s.s1.o.a: Siu: compare the numerator 7 with the 6 in 0.6
y-m-16-03.s.s1.r.a: This directly compared the numerator of a fraction with a digit of a decimal. A fraction with denominator 12 and 0.6 with denominator 10 are not in the same unit, so they cannot be compared this way.
y-m-16-03.s.s1.o.b: Hayoon: divide 7 by 12 to change it to a decimal and compare
y-m-16-03.s.s1.r.b: This changed the fraction into a decimal to make the same form and compared. It also matters whether the places were examined far enough that the difference between 0.583… and 0.6 is clear.
y-m-16-03.s.s1.o.c: Dohyun: change 0.6 to 3/5, find a common denominator, then compare the numerators
y-m-16-03.s.s1.r.c: This changed the decimal to a fraction and compared after making the denominators the same.
y-m-16-03.s.s1.o.d: Jihu: change 0.6 to a fraction with denominator 12 and compare the numerators
y-m-16-03.s.s1.r.d: Even if a numerator is not a natural number, you can compare once the denominators are made the same. It was not thrown away just because the form is unfamiliar.
y-m-16-03.s.s1.explain: The methods of Hayoon, Dohyun, and Jihu all compare after putting the two numbers into the same unit or the same form, so they are valid. Siu's method directly compares the numerator and a digit of numbers with different denominators, so it is not right (7/12 = 0.583… is less than 0.6). Hayoon's method needs to be calculated to the place where the difference can be seen, as with 0.583… and 0.6.
y-m-16-03.s.s2.prompt: About how many fractions are there that are greater than 0.6 and less than 3/4 in all?
y-m-16-03.s.s2.hint.0: Change 0.6 and 3/4 into the same form and write down which numbers fit between 0.6 and 0.75.
y-m-16-03.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how many times you can keep dividing the space between 0.6 and 0.75 into finer pieces.
y-m-16-03.s.s2.o.a: There are none. The two numbers are too close, so nothing can fit between them
y-m-16-03.s.s2.r.a: Change the values of the two numbers into decimals. Can you see the gap between 0.6 and 0.75?
y-m-16-03.s.s2.o.b: There is exactly one. It is only the one number exactly in the middle of the two numbers
y-m-16-03.s.s2.r.b: Besides the middle number, there are fractions like 7/10 and 2/3 between them. Compare their values one by one.
y-m-16-03.s.s2.o.c: Fractions and decimals are different forms, so you can't say which numbers lie between them
y-m-16-03.s.s2.r.c: Fractions and decimals differ only in form; they are numbers on the same number line. If you change them into one form, you can say what is between them.
y-m-16-03.s.s2.o.d: If you keep making the denominator bigger you can keep finding more, so there are endlessly many
y-m-16-03.s.s2.r.d: This used the fact that making the denominator bigger makes the marks of fractions finer.
y-m-16-03.s.s2.explain: If you make the denominator large, like 100, 1000, …, you can keep finding new numbers between 0.6 and 0.75, so there are endlessly many. In the next step you will look only for irreducible fractions whose denominator is 20 or less.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.prompt: Make 3 different irreducible fractions a/b that are greater than 0.6 and less than 3/4. (The numerator a and denominator b are natural numbers, and the denominator is 20 or less.)
y-m-16-03.s.s3.hint.0: First choose a denominator, then change the numerator and check whether the value is between 0.6 and 0.75.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.hint.1: Change the candidate to a decimal, or compare it by finding a common denominator with 3/5 and 3/4, and also check whether it can be reduced.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.ok.c1: The numerator and denominator are natural numbers and the denominator is 20 or less.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.fail.c1: The numerator and denominator must be natural numbers, and the denominator must be from 2 to 20.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.ok.c2: It cannot be reduced any further.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.fail.c2: The numerator and denominator have a common factor greater than 1, so it can be reduced.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.fail.c3: This fraction is not greater than 0.6. Compare its value with 0.6.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.fail.c4: This fraction is not less than 3/4. Compare its value with 3/4.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.explain: For example, 2/3 (0.666…), 7/10 (0.7), and 5/8 (0.625) are all greater than 0.6 and less than 0.75. 3/5 (=0.6) and 3/4 are the boundaries, so they are not between. 14/20 has the value 0.7, but it is a fraction that can be reduced.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.because.prompt: Write in one or two sentences how you could show a friend that the fraction you chose is greater than 0.6 and less than 3/4.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.because.hint.0: Change the fraction you chose into the same form as 0.6 (a decimal or the same denominator) and write it down.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.because.hint.1: Compare it with 3/4 in the same way too.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.because.placeholder: e.g. ... changed to a decimal is ..., so ...
y-m-16-03.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Can the method I wrote be used just the same for other fractions?
y-m-16-03.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check both that it is greater than 0.6 and that it is less than 3/4?
y-m-16-03.s.s3.because.model.0: 7/10 changed to a decimal is 0.7. 0.7 is greater than 0.6 and less than 0.75, so it is between the two.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.because.model.1: To write 5/8 as a decimal, I divided 5 by 8 and got 0.625. It is between 0.6 and 0.75, so it fits the conditions.
y-m-16-03.s.s3.because.model.2: If I put 2/3 over a common denominator of 12 with 3/4, it is 8/12 < 9/12, and with 3/5 over 15 it is 10/15 > 9/15. So 2/3 is between 0.6 and 3/4.

y-m-16-04.title: Working out how many gift boxes can be tied with the ribbon
y-m-16-04.topic: Division of decimals: interpreting a decimal quotient to fit the situation
y-m-16-04.goal: In a situation where the value of the division (19.5) alone does not fix the answer, find the information you need to know more, and make and explain cases where the answer changes depending on the information.
y-m-16-04.material: Tying one gift box needs 0.8 m of ribbon (including the length used for the knot). There are three pieces of ribbon, with lengths of 4.5 m, 5.1 m, and 6.0 m. The teacher asked, “How many boxes can be tied in all?” Hyoju divided 15.6 m, the sum of the three lengths, by 0.8 m, got the value 19.5, and answered, “About 19.”
y-m-16-04.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-16-04.thinking.1: Making cases where the answer changes depending on the assumption
y-m-16-04.prereq.1: Quotient and remainder in division (the experience of thinking about the meaning when the quotient is a decimal)
y-m-16-04.s.s1.prompt: Before trusting Hyoju's answer of ‘19 boxes,’ choose all the things you should first check with the teacher.
y-m-16-04.s.s1.hint.0: To answer ‘how many can be tied,’ you need to know how the ribbon is used. Imagine whether the answer could change if the way it is used changes.
y-m-16-04.s.s1.hint.1: For each question, check one by one whether its answer changes the ‘19 boxes’ or does not.
y-m-16-04.s.s1.o.a: Whether the ribbon pieces can be joined together to use
y-m-16-04.s.s1.r.a: If the pieces are joined, you can add the lengths and use them all; if they cannot be joined, you have to think about each piece separately. You pointed out information that affects the answer.
y-m-16-04.s.s1.o.b: Whether the ribbon left over after tying boxes can be used for other decorations
y-m-16-04.s.s1.r.b: Where the leftover ribbon is used has nothing to do with the number of boxes that can be tied. Think about whether it is information needed to decide the number.
y-m-16-04.s.s1.o.c: Whether any length is lost when the ribbon is cut with scissors
y-m-16-04.s.s1.r.c: If length is lost in cutting, the number of boxes using 0.8 m each could change. You pointed out an assumption.
y-m-16-04.s.s1.o.d: How much 1 m of ribbon costs
y-m-16-04.s.s1.r.d: The price is not used to find the number. Check again what you are trying to find.
y-m-16-04.s.s1.explain: Depending on whether the ribbon can be joined, you can use the value of 15.6 ÷ 0.8, or you may have to divide each piece separately. Whether length is lost when cutting also affects the number. What the leftover ribbon is used for and the price of the ribbon have nothing to do with how many can be tied.
y-m-16-04.s.s2.prompt: Suppose the ribbon cannot be joined and no length is lost when cutting. Choose the lengths p, q, r (m, to one decimal place, each at least 0.8 m) of the three pieces so that the sum is 15.6 m and the total number of boxes tied by cutting each piece separately is fewer than 19. Make 2 different cases.
y-m-16-04.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one piece and write how many times 0.8 m can be cut from it and how much is left.
y-m-16-04.s.s2.hint.1: Look at what the leftover lengths of the three pieces add up to, and check whether the leftovers gathered together are 0.8 m or more.
y-m-16-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The three pieces are at least 0.8 m and to one decimal place.
y-m-16-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Each of the three pieces must be at least 0.8 m and written only to one decimal place.
y-m-16-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the three pieces is 15.6 m.
y-m-16-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the three pieces is not 15.6 m.
y-m-16-04.s.s2.ok.c3: If each piece is cut separately, fewer than 19 boxes can be tied.
y-m-16-04.s.s2.fail.c3: With these pieces, you can tie 19 even when cutting each piece separately. Count how many times 0.8 m fits into each piece.
y-m-16-04.s.s2.explain: From 4.5 m you get 5 (0.5 m left), from 5.1 m you get 6 (0.3 m left), and from 6.0 m you get 7 (0.4 m left), 18 in all. If joined, 15.6 ÷ 0.8 = 19.5, so 19 can be tied. If the leftover ribbon of each piece is less than 0.8 m and cannot be used, the number goes down. Even with a sum of 15.6 m, 4.0 m, 5.6 m, and 6.0 m do not go down: 5 + 7 + 7 = 19.
y-m-16-04.s.s3.prompt: If the teacher asks again, “How many can be tied?”, write what you will check and then how you will answer. Write, with numbers, how the answer changes depending on what you checked.
y-m-16-04.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate separately how many there are for the case where the ribbon can be joined and the case where it cannot.
y-m-16-04.s.s3.hint.1: Before writing the answer, first write in one sentence ‘what you would need to check for the answer to be settled.’
y-m-16-04.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. First I will ask whether .... If ..., it is ... boxes, and if ..., it is ... boxes.
y-m-16-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write both cases in which the answer splits depending on what is checked?
y-m-16-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you show with numbers how you found the number in each case?
y-m-16-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you know and write the assumption that ‘no length is lost when cutting’?
y-m-16-04.s.s3.model.0: I will first ask whether the ribbon pieces can be joined together. If they can be joined, 15.6 ÷ 0.8 = 19.5, so 19 boxes; if each piece is cut separately, 5 + 6 + 7 = 18 boxes.
y-m-16-04.s.s3.model.1: I will ask whether the pieces may be joined and used. If they can be joined, 19 boxes can be tied; if they cannot be joined, it is 5 from 4.5 m, 6 from 5.1 m, and 7 from 6.0 m, 18 boxes in all.

y-m-16-05.title: Who walked faster?
y-m-16-05.topic: Division of fractions: comparing speed by distance and time
y-m-16-05.goal: Know that speed cannot be fixed when the time taken is unknown; when the time is given, change both to the same standard (the distance in one hour, or the time for 1 km) to compare, and revise your first thought.
y-m-16-05.material: Seoyun and Haram walked along the same road, each at a steady speed. You will be told the distance walked and the time taken, one piece at a time. 1/2 is read ‘one half’ and 3/4 is read ‘three fourths.’
y-m-16-05.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-16-05.thinking.1: Comparing by changing to the same standard
y-m-16-05.thinking.2: Revising your first thought with new information
y-m-16-05.prereq.0: How to multiply and divide fractions (6th-grade level)
y-m-16-05.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of fractions (common denominators)
y-m-16-05.prereq.2: Assuming that each walks at a steady speed
y-m-16-05.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose your thinking about who was faster.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.hint.0: Read each piece of information and write what is still missing in order to talk about speed.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.hint.1: Organize Seoyun's and Haram's distances and times in a table and calculate the values changed to the same standard.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.info: Seoyun walked 1/2 km and Haram walked 1/4 km. The time they took has not been told yet.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.after: Speed can be fixed only when both distance and time are present. When you know only the distance, the suitable judgment is ‘Seoyun might be faster, but we can't tell.’
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You spoke as if the two people took the same time. Nowhere does it say the times are the same.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Haram. Because the distance walked was shorter, so he must have arrived quickly
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: The arrival time and the time taken have not been told. We can't tell whether he arrived quickly because the distance was shorter.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The two have the same speed. Because both walked at a steady speed
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: ‘Each at a steady speed’ does not mean the two people's speeds are the same; it means each one's speed does not change.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.o.d: We can't fix it yet because we don't know the time taken
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You noticed that to fix speed you need time, not just distance.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.info: Seoyun walked for 3/4 hour, and Haram walked for 1/3 hour.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: Choose all the suitable ways to compare the two people's speeds.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.after: You can compare by putting everything on one standard. You can use the distance in one hour, or the time for going 1 km, and the results of the two ways must agree.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Compare only the time taken. Haram, whose time is shorter, is faster
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The distances are different, so you cannot compare only the times. Seoyun walked longer, but she also walked farther.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Change to the distance that can be covered in one hour and compare
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is a method that sets the time standard to 1 hour and compares distances.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Change to the time taken to go 1 km and compare (the shorter, the faster)
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a method that sets the distance standard to 1 km and compares times.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Add the distances together and the times together, then compare the values
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Adding the distances and times of two different people is useless for comparing speed.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.info: Calculating, Seoyun goes 2/3 km in one hour and takes 3/2 hours to go 1 km. Haram goes 3/4 km in one hour and takes 4/3 hours to go 1 km.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now who would you say walked faster? Compare with your first thought.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.after: 3/4 = 9/12 and 2/3 = 8/12, so Haram goes farther in one hour. The time for 1 km is also shorter for Haram (4/3 hours) than for Seoyun (3/2 hours). Seoyun's distance was longer but the time she took was also longer, so the first thought must be revised.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Seoyun. She walked farther at first, so she is still faster
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You did not compare your first judgment with the new information. Compare the distances in one hour.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Haram. In one hour he goes 3/4 km, more than Seoyun's 2/3 km
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You compared the values changed to the same standard and revised your first thought.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: They are the same. Both fractions are less than 1, so the speed is the same
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Being less than 1 is not enough to say the sizes are the same. Compare 3/4 and 2/3 by finding a common denominator.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.o.d: They did not walk for one hour, so the distance in one hour cannot be compared
y-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.r.d: If they walked at a steady speed, you can talk about the same speed even for time they did not walk.
y-m-16-05.s.s1.reflect: How did your first thought (‘Seoyun walked farther’) change when it met the information about time? Check whether the results compared by the distance in one hour and by the time for 1 km point the same way.
y-m-16-05.s.s2.prompt: To a friend who first thought ‘Seoyun walked farther, so she is faster,’ explain why it could not be fixed from the distance alone. Also write how you can compare.
y-m-16-05.s.s2.hint.0: Write Seoyun's and Haram's times side by side, and imagine which thought would have been right if the times had been the same.
y-m-16-05.s.s2.hint.1: First write in one sentence what you should make the same in order to compare.
y-m-16-05.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. From the distance alone ... the time ...
y-m-16-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write that both distance and time are needed?
y-m-16-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write the method of comparing by putting things on one standard?
y-m-16-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Does it show that you revised your first thought with the new information?
y-m-16-05.s.s2.model.0: You shouldn't look only at the distance. Seoyun walked 3/4 hour and Haram walked 1/3 hour, so the times are different. You have to change to the distance covered in one hour to compare.
y-m-16-05.s.s2.model.1: The times taken are different, so you can't decide from the distance alone. You have to compare by matching either how far they go in the same time or how long it takes to go the same distance.

y-m-16-06.title: Rewriting the notice about dividing the flour equally
y-m-16-06.topic: Division of decimals: deciding the place when the quotient is used as an approximation
y-m-16-06.goal: Decide to which place a quotient that does not end should be written, to fit the conditions of the situation (the scale's marks, the amount left over), and rewrite the notice so the person who receives it can understand.
y-m-16-06.material:
At a cooking contest, 7 kg of flour is to be divided equally among 3 teams. The scale can measure down to 0.01 kg (10 g). 7 ÷ 3 is 2.3333…, which does not end. The flour left over after each team takes theirs is taken by the helper in charge. The helper Mina wrote a draft of the notice.
Draft: “Each team, please take 2.3 kg of flour.”
y-m-16-06.thinking.0: Deciding the place of an approximation by the conditions of the situation
y-m-16-06.thinking.2: Writing a notice to suit the audience
y-m-16-06.prereq.0: Multiplication and division with numbers up to two decimal places
y-m-16-06.prereq.1: Writing the quotient of a non-terminating division as a decimal
y-m-16-06.s.s1.prompt: What happens if each team is given 2.3 kg as in the draft?
y-m-16-06.s.s1.hint.0: Multiply the amount for one team by the number of teams to find the total the three teams take.
y-m-16-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the total with 7 kg and check whether it falls short or is left over.
y-m-16-06.s.s1.o.a: The flour the three teams take exceeds 7 kg, so there will be too little
y-m-16-06.s.s1.r.a: If you calculate 2.3 × 3, it is less than 7. Multiply it yourself to check whether it falls short or is left over.
y-m-16-06.s.s1.o.b: The amount the three teams take is exactly 7 kg, so nothing is left over
y-m-16-06.s.s1.r.b: Calculate for yourself whether adding 2.3 kg three times makes 7.
y-m-16-06.s.s1.o.c: The amount the three teams take is 6.9 kg, so 0.1 kg is left over
y-m-16-06.s.s1.r.c: You multiplied the amount for one team by the number of teams to get the total taken, and compared it with 7 kg.
y-m-16-06.s.s1.o.d: One team will get less, so the amount differs from team to team
y-m-16-06.s.s1.r.d: It was decided that all teams take the same amount. Think about how, even with the same amounts, the total may not match.
y-m-16-06.s.s1.explain: 2.3 × 3 = 6.9, so out of 7 kg only 6.9 kg goes out and 0.1 kg (100 g) is left. If the scale can measure down to 0.01 kg, you can divide more precisely.
y-m-16-06.s.s2.prompt: Choose the amount q kg for one team as an amount the scale can measure (to two decimal places). Find 2 or more different values of q for which the total the three teams take does not exceed 7 kg and the leftover flour is 0.08 kg (80 g) or less.
y-m-16-06.s.s2.hint.0: First set q to 2.3 and find the three teams' share and the leftover amount, then change q by 0.01 at a time and see how it changes.
y-m-16-06.s.s2.hint.1: When you reach a case where the total the three teams take exceeds 7, put only the values up to just before it in as candidates.
y-m-16-06.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an amount with up to two decimal places.
y-m-16-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Write it as an amount with up to two decimal places, which the scale can measure.
y-m-16-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The amount the three teams take does not exceed 7 kg.
y-m-16-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The amount the three teams take exceeds 7 kg. There is not enough flour.
y-m-16-06.s.s2.ok.c3: The leftover flour is 0.08 kg or less.
y-m-16-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The leftover flour is more than 0.08 kg. Try increasing the amount for one team a little.
y-m-16-06.s.s2.explain: 2.31, 2.32, and 2.33 kg all fit the conditions. 3 × 2.31 = 6.93 (leftover 0.07 kg), 3 × 2.32 = 6.96 (0.04 kg), and 3 × 2.33 = 6.99 (0.01 kg). With 2.3 the leftover is 0.1 kg, and 2.34 gives 7.02 kg, which is too much.
y-m-16-06.s.s3.prompt: Instead of the draft, rewrite a notice to be read aloud to the team leaders. State exactly the amount of flour for one team, and add in one or two sentences why you chose that amount instead of 2.3 kg.
y-m-16-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write first the information the team leader reading the notice needs (how much to take).
y-m-16-06.s.s3.hint.1: For the reason, show once in numbers the total the three teams take and the leftover amount.
y-m-16-06.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. Each team, please take ... kg of flour. ...
y-m-16-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the amount clear, so that a team leader can read it and right away measure and take the same amount?
y-m-16-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain the difference between 2.3 kg and the amount you wrote using the total or the leftover amount?
y-m-16-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write it in words that the listeners can understand even if they are children?
y-m-16-06.s.s3.model.0: Each team, please take 2.33 kg of flour. If you measure to two decimal places, the three teams together take 6.99 kg and almost nothing is left over. With 2.3 kg each, 0.1 kg is left over.
y-m-16-06.s.s3.model.1: The amount of flour one team takes is 2.31 kg. If you do this, the three teams together take 6.93 kg, which does not exceed 7 kg, and the leftover is only 0.07 kg.
y-m-16-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: A value different from the rounded value (2.33), such as 2.31, is also valid if it fits the conditions.

y-m-16-07.title: Finding fractions that end at the second decimal place
y-m-16-07.topic: Relation between fractions and decimals: fractions that end when written as decimals
y-m-16-07.goal: Judge, by connecting it with the denominator, the place where the digits after the decimal point end when a fraction is written as a decimal, and make fractions that fit the conditions to state the rule about what denominators they have.
y-m-16-07.material: Soyul said, “When you write a fraction as a decimal, the bigger the denominator, the longer it gets after the decimal point.” (If the digits after the decimal point go on without end, it is said to be the longest.) You will check whether Soyul's statement is right and make fractions that end at two places after the decimal point when written as decimals.
y-m-16-07.thinking.0: Finding a counterexample to a claim
y-m-16-07.thinking.1: Estimating before writing a fraction as a decimal
y-m-16-07.thinking.2: Making examples that fit the conditions and finding a rule
y-m-16-07.prereq.0: Writing as a decimal by changing the denominator to 10 or 100
y-m-16-07.s.s1.prompt: Which example shows that Soyul's statement is not right?
y-m-16-07.s.s1.hint.0: Write Soyul's statement in one sentence, then imagine what two fractions would have to come out for the statement to be wrong.
y-m-16-07.s.s1.hint.1: Write each example as a decimal and compare which way the size of the denominator and the length after the decimal point go.
y-m-16-07.s.s1.o.a: 1/3 and 1/4: 1/4, with the bigger denominator, ends as 0.25, and 1/3 goes on without end
y-m-16-07.s.s1.r.a: The one with the smaller denominator is actually longer, so you found an example that goes against the statement.
y-m-16-07.s.s1.o.b: 1/2 and 1/4: 1/4, with the bigger denominator, is 0.25 with two places, so it is longer
y-m-16-07.s.s1.r.b: The one with the bigger denominator came out longer, so this example supports Soyul's statement. An example showing the statement is wrong has to come out the other way.
y-m-16-07.s.s1.o.c: 1/10 and 1/100: 1/100, with the bigger denominator, is 0.01 with two places, so it is longer
y-m-16-07.s.s1.r.c: The one with the bigger denominator came out longer, so it goes the same direction as Soyul's statement.
y-m-16-07.s.s1.o.d: 1/5 and 1/7: 1/7, with the bigger denominator, goes on without end as 0.142857…, so it is longer
y-m-16-07.s.s1.r.d: The one with the bigger denominator is longer, so this is an example in the same direction as Soyul's statement.
y-m-16-07.s.s1.explain: 1/3 = 0.333… goes on without end, but 1/4 = 0.25, with the bigger denominator, ends at two places. When the one with the smaller denominator is longer like this, Soyul's statement is not right. The other examples all go in the same direction as the statement, so they cannot be counterexamples.
y-m-16-07.s.s2.prompt: Without a calculator, looking only at whether the denominator can be made 10 or 100, choose all the fractions that end at two places after the decimal point.
y-m-16-07.s.s2.hint.0: For each fraction, find what natural number multiplied by the denominator makes 100.
y-m-16-07.s.s2.hint.1: For fractions that have such a number, multiply the numerator by the same number and write it as a decimal.
y-m-16-07.s.s2.r.a: The denominator 8 cannot be made 10 or 100. If you write 3/8 as a decimal, it continues to three places after the decimal point.
y-m-16-07.s.s2.r.b: The denominator 20 has a number that makes 100 when multiplied. You can make the denominator 100 and write it as a decimal.
y-m-16-07.s.s2.r.c: For the denominator 15, there is no natural number that makes 10 or 100 when multiplied. When written as a decimal, it goes on without end.
y-m-16-07.s.s2.r.d: Multiplying the denominator 25 by 4 gives 100. You can multiply the numerator by 4 too and write it as a decimal.
y-m-16-07.s.s2.explain: 7/20 = 35/100 = 0.35 and 9/25 = 36/100 = 0.36 end at two places after the decimal point. 3/8 is 0.375 with three places, and 4/15 is 0.2666…, which goes on without end.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.prompt: Make 3 different irreducible fractions a/b that end at exactly two places after the decimal point when written as decimals. (a is a natural number less than b, and the denominator b is 50 or less.)
y-m-16-07.s.s3.hint.0: First decide which numbers you can use as the denominator. Find numbers that divide 100 evenly.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.hint.1: With the denominator you chose, change the numerator and check whether the value of 100 times it divides evenly by the denominator.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.ok.c1: The numerator and denominator are natural numbers and it is a proper fraction.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.fail.c1: The numerator a must be 1 or more and less than the denominator b, and b must be a natural number of 50 or less.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.ok.c2: It cannot be reduced any further.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.fail.c2: The numerator and denominator have a common factor greater than 1.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.ok.c3: It is a fraction whose denominator can be made 100 (it ends within two places after the decimal point).
y-m-16-07.s.s3.fail.c3: It does not end at two places after the decimal point (it goes on without end, or has three or more places).
y-m-16-07.s.s3.ok.c4: It does not end at one place; it is exactly two places.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.fail.c4: It ends at one place after the decimal point. Look for fractions that have two places.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.explain: 1/4 = 0.25, 3/20 = 0.15, 9/25 = 0.36, and 7/50 = 0.14 all end at exactly two places. 1/2 (0.5) has one place, 3/8 (0.375) has three places, and 1/3 goes on without end. 6/20 is a fraction that can be reduced.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.because.prompt: Looking at the denominators of the fractions you made, write in one or two sentences what you found out about which denominators give fractions that end at two places after the decimal point.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.because.hint.0: Write all the denominators of the fractions you made, and calculate what happens when you divide 100 by those denominators.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.because.hint.1: Compare with the denominators that did not work (8, 15, etc.) and write what is different.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.because.placeholder: e.g. The denominators of my fractions were ..., and ...
y-m-16-07.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write that all the denominators of the fractions you made have the same property?
y-m-16-07.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you state the relation between 100 and the denominator?
y-m-16-07.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Can you explain why fractions with denominator 8 or 15 do not work?
y-m-16-07.s.s3.because.model.0: The denominators of my fractions are 4, 20, and 25, and all of them are numbers that divide 100 evenly. If the denominator can be made 100, it ends at the second decimal place.
y-m-16-07.s.s3.because.model.1: When the denominator is a factor of 100, like 4, 25, and 50, I could make the denominator 100, so I could write it with two places after the decimal point. 3 or 8 cannot be made into 100, so they don't work.

y-m-16-08.title: Testing Hajun's claim 'adding the same number leaves it the same'
y-m-16-08.topic: Comparing the sizes of fractions: changing the numerator and denominator together
y-m-16-08.goal: Judge the claim that adding the same number to the numerator and denominator leaves the size of a fraction unchanged, by looking at what kind of fractions the examples are, and use counterexamples to show how the size changes for fractions less than 1 and fractions greater than 1.
y-m-16-08.material: Hajun added 2 to both the numerator and the denominator of the fractions 4/4 (four fourths) and 7/7 (seven sevenths). They became 6/6 and 9/9, and both are 1, so the size stayed the same. Hajun said, “Even if you add the same number to the numerator and denominator of a fraction, the size of the fraction stays the same. It's like dividing by the same number when you reduce!”
y-m-16-08.thinking.0: Judging by looking at the kind of examples
y-m-16-08.prereq.0: Comparing the sizes of fractions (common denominators)
y-m-16-08.prereq.1: Knowing that reducing a fraction does not change its size
y-m-16-08.prereq.2: Meaning of proper fractions and improper fractions
y-m-16-08.s.s1.prompt: Looking at the examples Hajun checked, how will you judge Hajun's statement?
y-m-16-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write in what way the two fractions Hajun chose are the same kind.
y-m-16-08.s.s1.hint.1: Choose one fraction with a different numerator and denominator, add the same number, and compare before and after.
y-m-16-08.s.s1.o.a: Both examples were right, so the size will always stay the same, and there is no need to test more
y-m-16-08.s.s1.r.a: There are only two right examples, and you did not look at what kind of fractions the two examples are.
y-m-16-08.s.s1.o.b: Adding changes the numbers, so the size of the fraction seems like it would change, and Hajun's statement is wrong
y-m-16-08.s.s1.r.b: In Hajun's examples the size stayed the same. To be definite about all cases, more testing is needed.
y-m-16-08.s.s1.o.c: You can't compare the size of a fraction by adding to its numerator and denominator, so you can't judge
y-m-16-08.s.s1.r.c: You can calculate and compare the fractions before and after adding. It is not that they can't be compared.
y-m-16-08.s.s1.o.d: Both examples are fractions whose numerator and denominator are equal, so other fractions need to be tested too
y-m-16-08.s.s1.r.d: You looked at what kind of fractions the examples are and thought of the kind that was not tested.
y-m-16-08.s.s1.explain: 4/4 and 7/7 are both fractions whose value is 1, so even if you add the same number, it stays 1. Since a fraction whose numerator and denominator are different (like 2/3) has not been tested, you still can't say 'it is always so.'
y-m-16-08.s.s2.prompt: For a fraction a/b with numerator a and denominator b, make 2 different examples where (a+n)/(b+n), made by adding the same number n to the numerator and denominator, differs in size from a/b. One must be a fraction less than 1 (a is less than b) and the other a fraction greater than 1 (a is greater than b). (a, b, and n are natural numbers of 20 or less.)
y-m-16-08.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one proper fraction and one improper fraction, write the fractions after adding the same number, and compare their sizes by finding a common denominator.
y-m-16-08.s.s2.hint.1: Start with the added number n as 1 and compare the two fractions yourself.
y-m-16-08.s.s2.ok.c1: a, b, and n are natural numbers of 20 or less.
y-m-16-08.s.s2.fail.c1: a, b, and n must be natural numbers from 1 to 20.
y-m-16-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The size of the fraction is different before and after adding.
y-m-16-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The size of the fraction is the same before and after adding. Change to a fraction whose numerator and denominator are different.
y-m-16-08.s.s2.explain: Adding 1 to 2/3 gives 3/4, which is bigger (8/12 → 9/12). Adding 1 to 5/4 gives 6/5, which is smaller (25/20 → 24/20). The second example is a fraction greater than 1, so the direction of the change is opposite. As in Hajun's examples, if the numerator and denominator are equal, the size stays the same.
y-m-16-08.s.s2.because.prompt: In the two examples you made, write in one or two sentences how the size of the fraction less than 1 and the fraction greater than 1 each changed.
y-m-16-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Find a common denominator for each of the two fractions you made and write which is bigger, before or after adding.
y-m-16-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write one sentence each, separating the fraction less than 1 from the one greater than 1.
y-m-16-08.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. A fraction less than 1 ..., and a fraction greater than 1 ...
y-m-16-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write the change for both kinds (a fraction less than 1 and a fraction greater than 1)?
y-m-16-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you actually compare your examples by finding a common denominator?
y-m-16-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you connect it with the point that a fraction whose numerator and denominator are equal stays the same?
y-m-16-08.s.s2.because.model.0: Adding 1 to 2/3 gives 3/4, and 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12, so it got bigger. Adding 1 to 5/4 gives 6/5, and from 25/20 to 24/20 it got smaller. A fraction less than 1 gets bigger and a fraction greater than 1 gets smaller.
y-m-16-08.s.s2.because.model.1: The proper fraction 1/2 became 2/3 and got bigger, and the improper fraction 3/2 became 4/3 and got smaller. If it is less than 1 it gets bigger, and if it is greater than 1 it gets smaller.
y-m-16-08.s.s3.prompt: When is the size unchanged after adding the same number that is not 0 to the numerator and denominator of a fraction a/b?
y-m-16-08.s.s3.hint.0: Put the examples you made earlier and Hajun's examples side by side, and write what kind of fractions the examples with unchanged size were.
y-m-16-08.s.s3.hint.1: For each choice, choose one fraction, add the same number, and compare the sizes.
y-m-16-08.s.s3.o.a: When the numerator and denominator are equal
y-m-16-08.s.s3.r.a: If the numerator and denominator are equal, the value of the fraction is 1, and it stays 1 even if you add the same number.
y-m-16-08.s.s3.o.b: When the numerator is less than the denominator
y-m-16-08.s.s3.r.b: In this case the fraction gets bigger. Compare with 3/4, which is 2/3 plus 1.
y-m-16-08.s.s3.o.c: When the number added is even
y-m-16-08.s.s3.r.c: Even if the number added is even, 4/5, which is 2/3 plus 2, is different from 2/3. Whether the added number is odd or even does not matter.
y-m-16-08.s.s3.o.d: When the numerator is greater than the denominator
y-m-16-08.s.s3.r.d: In this case the fraction gets smaller. Compare with 6/5, which is 5/4 plus 1.
y-m-16-08.s.s3.explain: If the numerator and denominator are equal, the fraction is 1, and after adding the same number the numerator and denominator are still equal, so it is 1. If the numerator is less than the denominator it gets bigger, and if it is greater it gets smaller. The two examples Hajun first chose were this case.
